headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks; slim's privileged container tooling amplifies the pair.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystems, and nullclaw also uses MCP plus browser/web inputs, so attacker-controlled content can cross from one agent’s outputs into the other’s instruction stream. slim lacks MCP, but its CLI workflow can still consume files or command output. The shared-file pathway is plausible in default setups, though not proven.
conditions: IF nullclaw writes untrusted web or workspace content into ~/.nullclaw/workspace/ and slim reads that same directory
IF either agent treats file contents as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable automatic ingestion of shared files
Add provenance labels to inter-agent files
Review any file-based prompts before execution
requires-engineering: enforce sandboxed, read-only handoff channels

B_data_leakage.rationale: nullclaw touches API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, conversation history, and audit logs, while slim touches certificate private keys, environment variables, and registry credentials. Both have broad network egress and filesystem access, so sensitive material can be exposed if either agent uploads context or artifacts to external services. The pairwise leakage pathway is credible from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF either agent forwards workspace files or logs to a remote backend
IF both agents are run on the same host with shared secrets in accessible paths
mitigations: Store secrets outside shared workspaces
Restrict outbound network destinations
Rotate any credentials exposed to either agent
Use separate OS users for each agent
requires-engineering: add secret-redaction before upload

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem and execute shells; nullclaw can also modify git state and use MCP, while slim operates on container images and Docker-related artifacts. If they share a writable directory or repository, concurrent edits can corrupt state or overwrite each other’s outputs. The overlap is strong enough to treat as dangerous by default when co-located.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or workspace path
IF nullclaw and slim run concurrently without file locking
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize write operations
Use git worktrees or separate clones
Lock shared mutable files
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: nullclaw can generate web, webhook, and agent-card content that slim may consume while manipulating container artifacts, so one agent’s output can become the other’s input without a verification step. slim is not documented as blindly trusting outputs, but the workflow still permits downstream action on unverified text. This is an interaction risk, though not clearly irreversible by default.
conditions: IF slim uses nullclaw-produced text as authoritative build or remediation input
IF no human or automated verification step checks nullclaw outputs before slim acts
mitigations: Insert a review step between agents
Require schema validation on handoff files
Limit slim to read-only analysis of nullclaw output
Log and diff all inter-agent artifacts
requires-engineering: add policy checks for trusted-output boundaries

E_compliance.rationale: nullclaw explicitly handles conversation history, audit logs, and multiple secret classes, while slim handles certificate files, private keys, environment variables, and registry credentials. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, so a concrete jurisdictional breach cannot be proven; however, differing retention and secret-handling surfaces create a plausible compliance mismatch. Uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF either agent retains logs or artifacts longer than the other for the same sensitive data class
IF regulated data is routed through both agents without a shared DPA or retention policy
mitigations: Document retention for each agent
Exclude regulated data from one agent’s workspace
Purge logs after each run
Confirm jurisdiction and DPA coverage
requires-engineering: align compliance controls across both systems
